In their village above Mandi, Kamal began to notice small things about his daughter Mehak. She said she'd eaten at school, but her tiffin came home untouched. She cut her roti into tiny pieces and moved them around the plate. She grew anxious if dinner was late or cooked in ghee, and she had started walking the hill road alone every evening.
He also heard what the aunties said at the wedding: "Mehak has become so slim and pretty." He saw her face when they said it.
Kamal said nothing at the dinner table, in front of her brothers. That night he sat with her on the steps. "Beta, I've noticed food seems hard lately. You're not in trouble. I love you as you are. Will you come with me to see Dr Negi on Saturday?" Mehak picked at a thread, then gave a small nod.

qa.q: How did Mehak's tiffin come home?
qa.a: Mehak's tiffin came home untouched.

qa.q: What did Kamal feel when he saw Mehak's face at the wedding?
qa.a: Kamal felt worried, sensing that the aunties' comments about her being slim were affecting her.

qa.q: Why was talking on the steps better than at the dinner table?
qa.a: Speaking privately, away from her brothers, let Kamal show concern gently, say she wasn't in trouble and suggest seeing Dr Negi.

qa.q: What might food feel like for Mehak right now?
qa.a: Food seems stressful for Mehak, bringing anxiety when dinner is late or cooked in ghee, and something to hide.

grounding: A parent notices his teenager becoming secretive and anxious about eating amid comments about bodies, and chooses gentle private concern and a doctor.

At the secondary school in Leicester, PE teacher Sami Haddad noticed that Bilal had gone quiet at lunch. He sat with an apple and a bottle of water, and once Sami saw him throw his sandwich away untouched. In the changing room some boys teased each other about "getting shredded", and Bilal laughed along too loudly.
One day a boy called out in front of the class, "Bilal's gone skinny!" Sami stopped the lesson. "We don't comment on people's bodies here. Carry on."
After class, he asked Bilal to help carry the cones, just the two of them. "I've noticed lunch seems tricky lately. I'm not cross. I'm just worried about you." Bilal shrugged, eyes down. Sami said he'd like to talk with Bilal's parents and the school nurse, so a doctor could help if needed. Bilal hesitated, then said, "Okay. Just not in front of anyone."

qa.q: What did Sami see Bilal throw away?
qa.a: Sami saw Bilal throw his sandwich away untouched.

qa.q: What was Sami feeling when he spoke to Bilal after class?
qa.a: Sami was worried about Bilal, not cross, as he said himself.

qa.q: How did Sami respond when a boy shouted "Bilal's gone skinny!"?
qa.a: Sami stopped the lesson and said they don't comment on bodies, then later spoke to Bilal privately instead of in front of the class.

qa.q: Why might Bilal want it kept away from everyone else?
qa.a: Bilal likely feels embarrassed and anxious about his eating being noticed, especially after the public remark.

grounding: A teacher notices a teenager anxious and secretive about eating amid body comments, and responds with private concern and a route to a doctor.

passage: At the athletics academy hostel, coach Tushar noticed that Abhinav, fifteen, had stopped coming to the mess for dinner. He said he'd eaten in his room. At lunch he pushed food around his plate and got visibly tense when anyone offered him seconds. In the changing room, Tushar had heard the older boys joking about who was 'too heavy to sprint'. He didn't raise it in front of the team. After training, he asked Abhinav to help carry the hurdles and, once they were alone, said quietly, 'I've noticed you're skipping dinner, and you seem worried about food. I'm not angry. I'm concerned.' Abhinav stared at the track and said nothing, then nodded. That evening Tushar phoned his parents, and they booked a doctor's appointment for the weekend. The next morning he told the team that comments about bodies would stop.

qa.q: What did the older boys joke about in the changing room?
qa.a: Who was 'too heavy to sprint'.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he noticed Abhinav's changes?
qa.a: Tushar was worried and concerned, sensing Abhinav was anxious about food.

qa.q: Why did Tushar talk to Abhinav alone rather than in front of the team?
qa.a: Speaking privately avoided embarrassing Abhinav and made it easier for him to hear the concern without shame.

qa.q: How might Abhinav have experienced the changing-room jokes?
qa.a: He may have felt ashamed and anxious, taking the comments about heavy runners to heart.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing a teenager becoming secretive and rigid about eating amid body comments, and responding with private concern, parents and a doctor.

Dear Ojas,
I'm writing this because when I try to say it, it comes out wrong, and you leave the room.
Over the last two months I've noticed some things. You've started eating dinner alone in your room. You check every packet for what's in it and get very upset if I cook with oil. You weigh yourself every morning. And I heard your cousins at the wedding joking about your cheeks, and I saw your face.
I'm not angry, and I'm not going to comment at the dinner table or in front of anyone. I'm worried because I love you. I've booked an appointment with Dr Bhatt on Saturday, just to talk, and I'll come with you, or wait outside if you prefer.
You don't have to reply to this. Just know I'm on your side.
Mumma (Nandini)

qa.q: Who joked about Ojas's cheeks?
qa.a: The cousins at the wedding.

qa.q: What is Nandini feeling as she writes the letter?
qa.a: Nandini is worried and loving, anxious that talking face to face keeps going wrong.

qa.q: Why is a private letter a good choice here?
qa.a: It lets Nandini share the concern gently without public remarks, and lets Ojas read it without feeling cornered.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ojas may feel exposed and uneasy at first, but also relieved that Mumma noticed and is on Ojas's side.

grounding: Shows a parent noticing a teenager becoming secretive and rigid about eating after body comments, and offering gentle private concern and a doctor's visit.

passage: So I'm Sharmila, I teach Class 11 biology, and this is the thing that stuck with me this year. Arohi, one of my brightest, started changing around Diwali. Always a water bottle, never a lunch box. She'd get jittery if the class went near the canteen. And during a nutrition lesson, a boy made a joke about someone's thighs, and I saw her go completely still. I'll be honest, my first instinct was to say something in front of everyone about healthy eating. I'm glad I didn't. I shut the joke down and moved on. Then I asked her to stay back to help with charts, and when we were alone I said, 'I've noticed you're not eating lunch, and I'm worried about you.' She cried. I called her mother that evening, gently, and they saw a doctor the same week.

qa.q: What did Arohi always carry instead of a lunch box?
qa.a: A water bottle.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel after deciding not to speak in front of the class?
qa.a: Sharmila felt relieved and glad about holding back, knowing a public remark could have hurt Arohi.

qa.q: What did Sharmila do that others could learn from?
qa.a: Sharmila stopped the body joke, spoke to Arohi privately with concern, called her mother the same evening and supported a doctor's visit.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when the boy joked about thighs?
qa.a: She probably felt anxious and ashamed, going completely still in her seat.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a teenager's anxiety and rigidity about eating amid body comments, and choosing gentle private concern and a doctor over public remarks.

I teach Class 10 here, so I see the lunch hour every day. Since the term began, Naveen has been opening his tiffin, rearranging the chapati and closing it again. He carries a small notebook that he snaps shut when anyone passes. On Monday a boy joked loudly about Naveen's "new skinny look" and a few laughed. I didn't know what was going on inside him, and I still don't. But I stopped the joke on the spot, without making Naveen the topic, and later asked him to help me carry books to the staffroom. There I said only that I had noticed lunch seemed hard lately and that I cared. He shrugged, eyes wet. That evening I phoned his parents, gently, and suggested a visit to their family doctor.
Irawati, class teacher

qa.q: What does Naveen do with his tiffin at lunch?
qa.a: He has been opening his tiffin, rearranging the chapati and closing it again.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling after the joke at lunch, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Irawati was worried and protective; the teacher stopped the joke at once and then made a private chance to show care.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's private approach wiser than raising it in class?
qa.a: A quiet word and a call to the parents avoided shaming Naveen in public, and the doctor's visit brings in the right help.

qa.q: How might Naveen have experienced the teacher's words in the staffroom?
qa.a: He may have felt exposed but also noticed and cared for; he shrugged, but his eyes were wet.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a teenager becoming secretive and anxious about eating, stopping public body comments and choosing private concern and a doctor's advice.
